body.text: In late September a local council decision in a small town in Germany’s far east caught the attention of CNN, the Guardian and other media outlets around the world. Well over a month later, it’s still being talked about by federal politicians and other contributors to public debate in Germany.

What happened? In 2025, AKuBiZ, an anti-fascist organisation committed to drawing attention to the Nazi past in southeastern Saxony, proposed commissioning seven Stolpersteine — literally: stumbling stones — in Heidenau, a town of 17,000 by the river Elbe, fifteen minutes by local train from Dresden. A majority of Heidenau’s councillors not only rejected the idea; they voted to prohibit any further memorials of that kind.

The cobblestone-sized Stolpersteine are inserted level with the pavement, usually in front of houses where people once lived who were persecuted in Nazi Germany. Their names and other personal details are engraved on a ten-by-ten-centimetre brass plaque affixed to a concrete cube. More than 100,000 Stolpersteine have been laid since the early 1990s, most of them in Germany. Extensive research about the lives of the individuals concerned usually precedes the installation of these memorials.

The Cologne artist Gunter Demnig came up with this way of making pedestrians take notice of the victims of Nazi Germany. He is still involved in manufacturing and laying Stolpersteine. He implanted the first in front of the Cologne town hall on 16 December 1992 to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the so-called Auschwitz Decree, an order by SS head Heinrich Himmler to deport Sinti and Romani people to Auschwitz. That inaugural Stolperstein was engraved not with an individual’s name but with the first words of Himmler’s notorious order.

In 1994 and 1995, Demnig laid Stolpersteine in Cologne and Berlin for individuals, many of them Jews persecuted on account of their presumed “race,” without seeking official permission. Since 1997, however, no Stolperstein has been laid without the local authorities’ approval. The costs (€120 apiece) are usually covered by private donors or civil society organisations, but the Stolpersteine become the property — and responsibility — of the relevant municipality once they’re embedded in the footpath.

Demnig installed Heidenau’s first Stolperstein in August 2021. That memorial, in front of the town hall, commemorates the Social Democrat Paul Gröger, Heidenau’s mayor from 1924 to 1933. After the Nazis came to power, they removed him from office when he refused to hoist the Swastika flag. On 19 June 1933, Gröger was imprisoned in the nearby Hohnstein concentration camp. He was so badly maltreated there that he was unable to walk after his release three weeks later. On 27 August 1933, he committed suicide.

Initially, neither Heidenau’s mayor, the Christian Democrat Jürgen Opitz, nor its council were enthusiastic about the Stolpersteine concept. But in December 2019, only four of the five councillors of the far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD, which had won close to 30 per cent of the vote in the 2019 local elections, voted against the Stolperstein for Gröger.

Even before Demnig’s first visit to Heidenau, its council had dealt with another submission to lay Stolpersteine. This time, the five AfD representatives abstained and all other councillors voted in favour. In February 2023, he thus installed four more Stolpersteine, this time for members of a local Jewish family. Opitz commented: “We need these places to stumble in our thinking.”

Three years later, thirteen of the twenty councillors in attendance rejected the laying of any further Stolpersteine. That majority included all AfD representatives as well as several independents and Christian Democrats. Their motion called instead for the creation of a “memorial space for the victims of war, terror, dictators, expulsion and, in particular, National Socialism in Heidenau” at the local cemetery. The (non-elected) municipal administration recommended opposing the motion, while Opitz’s (elected) successor, an independent, supported it. Neither sought the views of the descendants of the seven people to be commemorated.

A memorial at the local cemetery would not be unheard of: particularly in the 1950s and 1960s, West German councils and municipal administrations often confined public memories of the Nazi past to graveyards. And there was nothing unusual about the idea of creating an all-purpose memorial for all victims, which potentially erases the distinction between perpetrators and their victims.

The Central Memorial of the Federal Republic of Germany for the Victims of War and Tyranny in Berlin could serve as the blueprint for what the majority of Heidenau’s councillors envisage. Dedicated in 1993, it replaced East Germany’s Memorial for the Victims of Fascism and Militarism. At the suggestion of then-chancellor Helmut Kohl, its centrepiece is a grotesquely enlarged pietà, Käthe Kollwitz’s sculpture Mother with Her Dead Son, which commemorates Germany’s war dead and the victims of Nazi Germany and those persecuted in communist East Germany.

Some of the arguments put forward in favour of banning new Stolpersteine in Heidenau are curious. One councillor conjured the prospect of “gilded streets,” prompting the local newspaper to point out that Heidenau’s public roads and footpaths have a combined length of 130 kilometres and twenty Stolpersteine would cover a mere 0.2 square metres. Another was afraid that pedestrians, who couldn’t literally stumble over Stolpersteine, would slip on them in winter.

The council decision also attracted attention because of Heidenau’s track record. In August 2015 violent protests against the accommodation of refugees there became emblematic of the dark underside of Germany’s much-celebrated Willkommenskultur, or culture of welcome. Demonstrators abused Opitz as a Volksverräter (traitor to the people), and engaged for two nights in battles with the police. Earlier, the area had been a stronghold of the National Democratic Party, a neo-Nazi outfit twice represented in Dresden’s state parliament. And in the 2017 elections Heidenau was in one of only three federal electorates where the AfD candidate topped the vote.

The council vote’s timing also explains why it made headlines: it came four days after the Christian Democrats had won less than 5 per cent of the vote in state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — the first time its vote had fallen so low in the history of the Federal Republic. The disastrous result prompted leading Christian Democrats to question their party’s agreed stance vis-à-vis the AfD. It had become counterproductive, they argued, to categorically rule out collaborating with the far right.

But the events in Heidenau provided welcome ammunition to those defending the Brandmauer, or fire wall, the democratic parties have put up to keep the AfD in check. Didn’t the Heidenau decision demonstrate what could happen if the conservatives voted with the far right? And didn’t the AfD’s agitation against Stolpersteine prove the party promoted dangerous historical revisionism at best, and, at worst, that it was itself a new Nazi party?

How representative was the ban imposed in Heidenau? The council of Germany’s third-largest city Munich has long been opposed to Stolpersteine on publicly owned footpaths. Supported by the city’s Jewish community, it favours plaques affixed to buildings. Germany’s second-largest city Hamburg, meanwhile, last month celebrated the twentieth anniversary of an initiative to compile biographies of the more than 7500 people commemorated with Stolpersteine there.

True, some people have taken issue with Demnig’s memorials. In the East German town of Bautzen, for example, activists were pestered and insulted by passers-by last year when they were cleaning Stolpersteine to mark the anniversary of the nationwide pogrom of 9–11 November 1938. But that was an exception. All over Germany this week, volunteers once again cleaned and polished tens of thousands of Stolpersteine, lit candles and put flowers on them.

Yes, some memorials have been vandalised or stolen. But those have been comparatively isolated incidents. And when all ten Stolpersteine in Zeitz (Saxony-Anhalt) disappeared two years ago, the municipal authorities received over a thousand donations totalling €52,800 — many times more than was needed to replace the memorials.

Stolpersteine have generally continued to be installed without attracting undue controversy. On 2 September, for instance, eleven new Stolpersteine were laid in Hermeskeil, a town of 6500 in the Hunsrück, an upland bounded by the rivers Rhine, Moselle, Saar and Nahe in the far west of Germany. Hermeskeil had gotten its first three Stolpersteine in 2006. The new ones commemorate the lives of members of the Ackermann and Samuel families, who lived in Hermeskeil until the 1930s. Students from the local high school were involved in the accompanying research.

One of Hermeskeil’s new Stolpersteine is located in front of a shop, Sport Fuchs. Its website recounts when it was founded and why it prospered: “For over eighty years, the shoe and sportswear store Fuchs has been a fixture in Hermeskeil. When the business was acquired in 1939 by Anna Fuchs, the grandmother of the current owner, it was a small shoe shop. During the war, good footwear was in high demand.”

The shop was once known as Schuhhaus Lieser. In 1938, its owner Ernst Samuel was appointed head of Hermeskeil’s Jewish congregation. In the course of the November 1938 pogroms, local residents not only ransacked the Hermeskeil synagogue but also smashed Schuhhaus Lieser’s windows. Samuel was arrested and deported to the Dachau concentration camp. His house and business became the property of the Hermeskeil municipality, which in turn sold them to Anna Fuchs.

Meanwhile, Ernst’s mother Helene was forcibly relocated to a so-called Judenhaus (Jews’ house) in nearby Trier. She was deported to the Theresienstadt ghetto in 1942 and then, two years later, taken to Auschwitz, where she was murdered on 15 May 1944.

After his release from Dachau, Ernst Samuel fled to Luxembourg. After the war, he emigrated to the United States and from there fought for the restitution of his property. Eventually he agreed to an out-of-court settlement with the shop’s new owner.

I know all this because of a text about the Samuels on a website dedicated to Hermeskeil’s Jewish history. The article’s co-author, Shida Bazyar, is depicted on a photo published in a local magazine and taken a day before the laying of the Stolpersteine, when an exhibition about the Ackermann family was opened at a local museum. The panels make use of correspondence Bazyar unearthed at Yad Vashem: letters between Frieda and Otto Ackermann and their daughter Cäcilie, who had fled to Denmark and survived the Holocaust. Her parents did not.

Shida Bazyar has since become famous well beyond Hermeskeil. She is the author of the novel Die Lücken, which won this year’s German Book Prize, Germany’s most prestigious literary award, as well as the 2026 Bavarian Book Prize and the Wilhelm Raabe Literary Award.

Readers interested in contemporary German literature already knew about Bazyar. Die Lücken is her third novel, and the two earlier books had already appeared in an English translation. The first, published in 2016 as Nachts ist es leise in Teheran and in translation by Melbourne publisher Scribe as Nights Are Quiet in Tehran (2025) was shortlisted for the 2026 International Booker Prize. Next year, Scribe will publish Ruth Martin’s translation of Die Lücken.

Bazyar lives in Berlin but is a native of Hermeskeil. She was born in 1988, the year after her parents arrived in the small Hunsrück town as political refugees from Iran. After finishing high school in Hermeskeil, she left to study creative writing at the University of Hildesheim.

Die Lücken is set in a fictional place, but it’s no secret that Bazyar modelled the novel’s Heimesbach on Hermeskeil. Some of Hermeskeil’s former residents even appear with their real names: Gustav Simon, for example, the most senior Nazi official of the Trier district, who had been a school teacher in Hermeskeil; and the Ackermanns, who, in the novel, on 27 July 1942 send a postcard to their erstwhile neighbours: “One hour before our departure we offer you our heartfelt thanks for your kind sympathy! May God reward you for it. Farewell!” Paraphrasing a line from the Gospel of Matthew, Otto Ackermann adds a postscript: “Whatever you did to the least of my brothers, you did to me.”

“The central characters and plot elements of this novel are fictional,” Bazyar says in her acknowledgements, but that’s not true of all of them. On the day Otto and Frieda Ackermann were deported from Trier to the Theresienstadt ghetto, they did write to their former Hermeskeil neighbours, the Eiden-Eidens, expressing their gratitude and bidding them good-bye.

When corresponding with their daughter in Denmark, Bazyar writes in the novel, the Ackermanns had mentioned “travels” that were coming up, but had otherwise talked about being busy. But with their former neighbours they didn’t need to pretend: “Earlier they greeted each other, in the street, every day, casually. Today they said good-bye one last time.”

The novel’s first-person narrator, who knows about the Ackermanns and has seen the postcard, has no name. She was presumably a refugee, moved to Heimesbach when she was ten, was resettled in the United States aged thirteen (“because they wanted to send us away”) and died young when a truck hit her as she was riding her bicycle.

Like Toni Morrison’s Beloved, she has a second life as a spirit. The gods send her back to Heimesbach to observe from above its inhabitants in the past and in the present. She can’t always see clearly; sometimes the images become blurred. And sometimes the gods suddenly cut short her observations and make her watch a different scene, in another era. Rather than addressing the reader, the narrator tells her sister Lu, who is two years older, what she is finding about the town that shaped them both although they hadn’t stayed long.

The narrator is surprised by what she learns about Heimesbach: how, in the 1930s, its Jewish residents were ostracised, robbed and driven out; how some of the perpetrators were never convicted and continued to live in Heimesbach after Nazi Germany’s defeat; and how, for decades, almost everybody remained silent about the persecution of their former Jewish neighbours.

In the 1930s, Hermeskeil was a typical German village, and after it was declared a town in 1970, it was like numerous other small towns in West Germany. There were thousands of Hermeskeils in Nazi Germany, towns where the local Jewish population was disappeared, with the tacit if not active support of a majority of non-Jewish Germans. But Hermeskeil was also special. In about 1936 it was named a Gaumusterdorf, or model village, with a new market square and new buildings to show how a village in Nazi Germany ought to look. And in 1938, earlier than elsewhere, Hermeskeil became “judenfrei,” a term used by the Nazis for areas where all Jewish residents had been forcibly removed.

The narrator tells her sister about Heimesbach’s record. But she is neither morally outraged nor does she consider herself superior to Heimesbach’s non-Jewish Germans. Her tone is sometimes sarcastic, sometimes mournful, but mostly matter-of-fact. The two sisters are not from Heimesbach and spent only three years in the Hunsrück. Their emotional investment in its past is limited. The histories that preoccupied them at the time related to the country they had fled.

During their time in Heimesbach it was its present rather than its history that bothered them. “Either they have sent me there by accident, or I have ended up in Hell,” the narrator remembers thinking. But she was safe, and that was all that mattered to her then. With the benefit of hindsight, however, she realises: “If we had known all these things from day one — not only sensed, but known — it would have made one difference: We would have known from the beginning that they would send us away as soon as they could.”

The novel’s structure is complex. Texts ostensibly written by the unnamed narrator alternate with chapters set at various times between the 1920s and the 2010s. They are not in chronological order and feature a large cast, including Heimesbach’s Jewish residents, its non-Jewish German residents, and two Iranian families who are resettled in Heimesbach in the 1980s and 1990s. Readers need to be particularly attentive: a girl first introduced only with her first name in an episode set in the 1920s may reappear, under her surname, in a chapter set decades later. Over the course of almost five hundred pages, a kaleidoscopic picture of Heimesbach and its residents emerges.

I couldn’t empathise with any of the novel’s non-Jewish German characters. That’s perhaps unsurprising in the case of perpetrators and bystanders. But one of the least likeable protagonists, for me, was Tobias, a young man who in 1990 studies to become an art teacher. He decides to create an artwork based on what his grandfather can tell him about the Nazi years. But he asks the wrong questions and can’t correctly read the answers. When he enquires about Hermeskeil’s Jews, the grandfather replies that “nobody was deported from Heimesbach’s railway station. That all happened later. Heimesbach was the first place in the region that became judenfrei.” Tobias notes that there was neither pride nor regret in the grandfather’s voice, but doesn’t persevere with his questions even when the grandfather volunteers information about when all the other villages in the region were declared judenfrei.

Die Lücken is about people who are variously gullible, egotistical, cruel and timid. Above all, it is a novel about indifference. It was indifference that made Nazi Germany’s murderous regime possible. And it was indifference towards the fate of its victims that characterised Germans’ response to the crimes perpetrated between 1933 and 1945, at least until the 1980s. As the example of Heidenau shows, indifference, rather than an outright denial of past wrongs, sometimes marks even today’s response.

Absolutely nobody cared about the stains, Bazyar lets the narrator say. “After the dictatorship of the National Socialists, a dictatorship of indifference took sway here.” She watches Emil Ackermann, the son of Frieda and Otto, who had managed to flee to Palestine, return to Heimesbach to visit the Jewish cemetery. It had been vandalised, first in 1929 and then in 1938, when the gravestones were not only overturned but removed for good. When Emil first visits, the cemetery, “which others had sought, with such violence, to destroy again and again” is overgrown. “[It] has now been left to the mercy of indifference. There is no yardstick for humiliations. Yet indifference is underrated as a form of insult.”

Later the municipality arranges for the cemetery to be cleaned up. But, as the narrator tells her sister, we ought to be suspicious of such arrangements. “When an area is mowed — in a way that feels like clearing land — things that no longer exist are brought back to light. The graves have long gone; that goes without saying. A mowed meadow promises order, and order means that someone cares. Someone is in charge. People love it when someone is in charge.”

In the book’s acknowledgments, Bazyar singles out two authors whose books inspired her. Eight years ago, the first, Heinz Ganz-Ohlig, published a detailed history of Hermeskeil’s Jewish community, which has just been reissued. Bazyar explains that Ganz-Ohlig’s project was prompted by a scandal, “one of many quiet, everyday scandals in a country that styles itself a world champion of remembrance:” When the local high school celebrated its centenary, it did not acknowledge its former Jewish students. Ohlig conducted research “to fill these voids, these gaps.”

What I have translated as “gaps,” is Lücken in Bazyar’s text. Lücken refers to things missing, stories never told, events not remembered. The gaps highlighted by Bazyar relate to specific parts of Heimesbach’s history. “Heinz Kahn possesses a very precise understanding of these gaps,” she writes. Kahn once lived in Hermeskeil, where his father was the local vet. He was deported with his parents and sister, but against all odds he survived more than two years in Auschwitz and Buchenwald. After his liberation, he moved to Trier, the city closest to Hermeskeil, where he re-established a Jewish congregation. Like his father, he became a vet, practiced near Koblenz, and for many years served as the chair of Koblenz’s Jewish congregation.
“I wish you could see what I can see from above,” the narrator tells her sister.

All the intricate entanglements and connections: which merchant took over what, from whom and when; who opened a business at what point; who went bankrupt… It was a process of giving and taking, of inheriting and passing on. And of theft. For every single one of the forty-two Jewish men and women living here in 1933 was robbed, regardless of whether they ran shops or dealt in livestock, and whether they were forced to flee, managed to survive or were murdered.

To fill these gaps, Bazyar seems to suggest, one needs to approach history with a forensic attention to detail: follow the money, make an inventory of the stolen property and trace how each item ended up with its current owner. How much exactly did Anna Fuchs pay for Schuhhaus Lieser? What happened to the shop’s stock, which, according to her son, had disappeared by the time she acquired the business? How much did she pay Ernst Samuel after the war in the out-of-court settlement?

Bazyar didn’t just rely on Ganz-Ohlig’s book; she did her own archival research and conducted interviews with Hermeskeil residents. Her book is an attempt to fill gaps, to remind non-Jewish Germans of something they forgot or pretend not to know. But she uses the term Lücken also in the sense of absences that can’t be undone, tears that can’t be mended. For every murdered Heimesbach Jew there was a “gaping Lücke in the air,” the narrator tells Lu. “It’s as if something had been snatched from the air. Perhaps that is why it is so difficult to breathe when one goes for a walk in this place; perhaps that is why every silence is an assertion, but no one is honest enough to say it out loud.”

Die Lücken is not the first German novel about villagers who drive out their Jewish neighbours and ostensibly fail to remember having done so after 1945. In 1979, Peter O. Chotjewitz published Saumlos, a novel about a village of that name in eastern Hesse. Much like Bazyar’s readers know that Heimesbach is Hermeskeil, his readers could easily identify Saumlos as Rhina, today one of five villages that form the municipality of Haunetal. Chotjewitz and his wife Renate Häfner-Chotjewitz lived in a neighbouring village, and found out that in the 1920s, Rhina had been the only village in Prussia where the majority of residents were Jewish.

In Saumlos, Chotjewitz draws attention to Rhina’s Jewish past. Unlike Bazyar, who benefited from Ganz-Ohlig’s research, Chotjewitz could not draw on the work of a local historian. He and his wife therefore did the necessary historical research themselves. They co-authored two radio features (later turned into a book) and a montage-like non-fiction text about Rhina, in which diary entries of a 1979 trip to Israel, where they interviewed some of Rhina’s former Jewish residents, alternate with biographical sketches, short chapters about Rhina’s Jewish community and archival documents.

Saumlos was only moderately successful — perhaps because it lacked the literary qualities of books like Die Lücken, or perhaps because of Chotjewitz’s left-wing politics — but its publication was timely. The fortieth anniversary of the 1938 pogroms had drawn attention to the persecution of Jews in Nazi Germany. More important, two-and-a-half months later the four-part American mini-series Holocaust (which first brought Meryl Streep to the attention of a global audience) was screened on West German television. Every second adult in West Germany watched at least one episode. It had a huge impact on how the Nazi past was publicly remembered.

Saumlos also responded to efforts among the West German left in the late 1970s to appropriate a term that had long been associated with Nazi ideology and with rural settings not yet affected by modernity: Heimat. The word is sometimes translated as homeland or home, although neither term has the same affective connotations Heimat carries in German.

In the 1950s and 1960s, Heimat was associated with a conservative, even backward-looking view that imagined a world that was still the way it used — and ought — to be. German, Austrian and Swiss movies and novels belonging to the genres Heimatfilm and Heimatroman, respectively, depicted an idyllic and innocent countryside. Their plots always ended happily. Writers like Chotjewitz tried to show an alternative rural Heimat: narrow-minded, full of repressed violence, replete with histories that could not be told. Their books became known as Anti-Heimatromane.

At the same time, Heimat was rediscovered as a place where people rebelled against nature’s overexploitation and fought to save the natural environment. The people of Wyhl in the southwest of Germany became the most prominent protagonists of a progressive Heimat movement when their 1970s protests prevented the construction of a nuclear power plant next to their village. With West Germans on the left unable to identify with a German nation, the idea of a local Heimat seemed to offer the option of a deep-seated attachment to a place whose culture was sufficiently specific not to be taken as representative of Germany as a whole.

Gerd Fuchs’s Stunde Null, published two years after Saumlos, is another prominent example of an Anti-Heimatroman. Fuchs is the second author singled out by Bazyar in her acknowledgements. He too grew up in Hermeskeil. His mother Anna Fuchs took over Ernst Samuel’s shoe shop. His father, headmaster of a vocational school, was in charge of the Nazis’ local propaganda division until he had a stroke in 1938. Like Bazyar, Gerd Fuchs wrote fiction that features the Nazi years and their aftermath in his home town.

In Heimwege, a memoir of sorts published in 2010, Fuchs recalls how some fifty years earlier he had attended a show by the actor Wolfgang Neuss: “He railed against this society — against its stupidity, its self-righteousness, its brutality and the carefree attitude with which it returned to business as usual after all those murders.” Fuchs could have been talking about his own writing. He too could not forgive Germans for how readily they carried on after 1945 as if nothing had happened.

In his 1981 novel Stunde Null, Fuchs writes about the months after the end of the war. The novel is set in Hermeskeil, where Fuchs’s family had moved in 1935 when he was three. Stunde Null is an angry book. The title, which means “Zero Hour,” refers to the lie that Nazi Germany’s surrender extinguished all debts and allowed for a new beginning. Fuchs shows how any attempt to hold the local supporters of the Nazi regime accountable is doomed to fail. Much like Die Lücken, his book engages with a local legacy. Fuchs was twelve when the war ended, so he may have been too young to remember the Ackermanns and the Samuels. But he would have been only too aware of Hermeskeil’s “intricate entanglements.”

In his memoir, Fuchs refers to the burning of the Hermeskeil synagogue. He misremembered: the building where the local shul was housed was ransacked during the 1938 pogrom but not set on fire, presumably to protect the adjoining buildings. It was later destroyed in an allied bombing raid. Fuchs’s incorrect reference suggests that he didn’t go to great lengths to research the local aspects of the Holocaust. Unlike Die Lücken, Stunde Null imagines acts of defiance during the Nazi years, with a non-Jewish German family harbouring, and thus saving Fräulen Stern, a young Jewish woman from Berlin.

In Fuchs’s novel, the local inhabitants are implicated in the Nazi period, and some of them prosper during and after, but “all those murders” happened, above all, in the East. The two main protagonists, a teenager and his older brother, talk about two photographs the former had found in a dead soldier’s wallet. “In one of the photographs, a long row of old men, women — and, it seemed to him, children too — could be seen hanging from a beam. In another, there were more old people, women, and children — along with a few younger men — standing at the edge of a pit.” Somebody had written “Russia, in October” on the back. The brother who had served as a soldier explains: “These people were either Jews, partisans — or taken to be partisans — or perhaps hostages.”

When asked whether he too had taken part in such killings, the older brother says: “Not directly. That sort of thing was usually carried out by the SS or the Feldpolizei [secret military police]. But we knew about it. After all, we were the ones who rounded the people up for them.” In 1981, his response ought to have made readers sit up and take notice. It wasn’t until the second half of the 1990s that the myth of the “clean” German army was shattered by a travelling exhibition put together by the Hamburg Institute for Social Research.

At the same time as Fuchs was writing a novel about his Hunsrück Heimat, the filmmaker Edgar Reitz sketched the outlines of a script for a ten-hour film about the people of a fictional Hunsrück village. The film was partly to provide an explanation for why Reitz, who had grown up in Morbach, a village twenty-five kilometres northeast of Hermeskeil, had left the Hunsrück to become a filmmaker.

Holocaust provided the prompt for Reitz’s exposé. He intended his film to be a German response to the American TV series, which he regarded as “designed solely to whip the audience into an emotional frenzy.” Holocaust’s family saga employed “every cliché of the sentimental melodrama,” he said, and didn’t allow its characters “a life of their own, complete with contradictions and human vulnerabilities.”

A producer working for one of West Germany’s public broadcasters liked Reitz’s idea, but suggested that it was more suitable for television than for the big screen. He was horrified when Reitz told him that he wanted to call the project “Heimat.” The producer thought the term “insufferably petty bourgeois and sentimental, and burdened by Nazi ideology, the false idyll of the Heimatfilm, pseudo-folklore, and tourist kitsch.” They agreed to use “Made in Germany” as the project’s working title, but eventually the broadcaster funding the film agreed to the title originally suggested by Reitz.

In June 1984, Heimat — presented as a fifteen-and-a-half hour film depicting the lives of an extended family in the fictional village Schabbach, told chronologically from 1919 until 1982 — premiered in a Munich cinema. In September and October 1984, Germany’s public broadcaster screened it as an eleven-part series. It became a success, also internationally. I remember watching it in August 1985 in a packed cinema in Canberra, where it was shown in four parts over two days. Reitz later made two sequels, one set in Munich in the 1960s and informed by the film-maker’s own experiences, and another set in the Hunsrück and featuring the same family as in the first Heimat film, which took their story until 2000.

Heimat counts as an Anti-Heimatfilm. With texts such as Saumlos and Stunde Null, it shares a critical view of life in the village. It highlights how most Germans were first implicated in the crimes of Nazi Germany and then pretended that they hadn’t happened. But like the earlier Heimatfilme, Heimat also offers a nostalgic take on rural life and sometimes idealises the seemingly “traditional” dispositions of some of its protagonists, which are ostensibly untainted by modernity and urban life.

While cinema and television audiences embraced Heimat and identified with some of its characters, the critics were divided, particularly outside Germany. Those who condemned the series did so because they thought Reitz had deliberately omitted the Holocaust and thus produced a revisionist history. “In order to tell the myth of ‘Heimat’ the trauma of Auschwitz has to be bracketed from German history,” declared one the film’s fiercest critics, New York film scholar Gertrud Koch. That’s arguably unfair for two reasons: she criticised the film not for what it was, but for what it was not (but she thought should have been), and Reitz’s notion of Heimat was twice removed from a German pastoral idyll.

Reitz later claimed that he had wanted to call the film not Heimat but rather Geheischnis. That’s a word from the Hunsrück dialect that is as untranslatable into German as Heimat is into English. According to Reitz, it means “a sense of security and human closeness. It originates from the realm of agriculture. It is related to the word Gehege [enclosure]: the demarcated space where humans and livestock live.” For him, the word was a local version of Heimat and affectively charged; it also referred to “the sleeping habits and bedtime rituals of Mother’s childhood, and the apples and pears in the neighbour’s garden before the first world war.”

Almost thirty years after Reitz’s monumental series, the term Heimat experienced another twist. In 2013, the Bavarian finance ministry was renamed Bayerisches Staatsministerium der Finanzen und für Heimat. Since then, it has been also responsible for the development of rural and regional Bavaria, including the promotion of local cultural traditions. Today, the ministry’s website claims that it is principally concerned with the living conditions, traditions and culture of the people of Bavaria, and that the preservation and further development “of this diversity of traditions is a key part” of its mandate.

When Angela Merkel offered Bavarian state premier Horst Seehofer the federal home affairs ministry in 2018, he insisted that it be renamed to include the interior, housing and Heimat. In 2025, the responsibility for Heimat was taken over by the minister for agriculture. In 2017, the state government in North Rhine-Westphalia also created a Heimat ministry.

In the first half of the 2010s, when the national conversation was dominated by liberals living in Germany’s ethnically and culturally diverse urban centres, Seehofer and other conservatives rediscovered Heimat as the antithesis to cosmopolitanism and multiculturalism. More recently, the AfD appropriated the concept. “A village is… Heimat, community and tradition,” says the 2026 election manifesto of Saxony-Anhalt’s AfD, which is likely to form government next month. It wants the state constitution to be amended to provide that “children are to be educated in the spirit of love for their Heimat and the German people.”

Bazyar’s Die Lücken hit German bookshops on 3 September. Its initial print-run of 60,000 was not enough to meet the demand. The book has now sold more than 120,000 copies and is in its seventh printing. When it won the German Book Prize on 5 October it topped Der Spiegel’s hardcover fiction bestseller list. Bookshops now wanting to host a reading with Bazyar are told that the earliest available date is in the second half of 2027.

The book’s commercial success is partly the result of the award it received last month. Previous German Book Prize winners also sold well over 100,000 copies. When Antje Rávik Strubel’s Blaue Frau won the prize five years ago, it jumped within a week from sixty-third to second on the Spiegel list. But the sales figures of Die Lücken also reflect the enthusiastic response of reviewers and readers to its perceived message.

The novel is a literary masterpiece. I want to read it again, the sooner the better. (It’s a long time since I last thought that about a novel.) The prizes it has already won are well deserved. But those aside, Bazyar also seems to have struck a nerve with the book’s subject matter. At first sight, this is surprising. The book’s message is not conciliatory; Bazyar doesn’t excuse the cruelty and indifference of her German protagonists. There is no hero or heroine for readers to readily identify with. There is no young Jewish woman who is rescued by a couple of upright non-Jewish Germans. The narrative’s ending is not redemptive. It does not allow its readers to reassure themselves of their own righteousness.

But perhaps the book’s presumed message cancels all that out. The blurb claims that Bazyar’s novel is a “literary archaeology of Heimat” which provides “a narrative about the burden of history, the lie of a ‘fresh start,’ and the longing to finally find a Heimat.” According to the announcement of a reading in Hamburg last month, “Bazyar poses a radical question: What are the foundations upon which we can build our Heimat?” Although the author insisted “Heimat is a completely empty term” for her, reviewers hail the book as a successful Heimatroman, or at least a book that makes a meaningful contribution to conversations about Heimat.

That’s not to say Bazyar’s novel isn’t also about the feeling of being at home. In a scene set in 1995, Parvaneh, who came to Heimesbach as a refugee, accidentally refers to her homeland, Iran, as “my Heimesbach,” rather than “my Heimat.” Her German guests are delighted, because to them it sounds as if Heimesbach has become home for Parvaneh. But she thinks that “Heimesbach was not a true home… the two words simply happened to lie side by side… In any case, she could only truly perceive a place as Heimat if she applied the [Farsi] term Watan to it; otherwise, it remained merely a word, an empty shell, something entirely interchangeable.”

Parvaneh’s guests then talk about the term Edgar Reitz has been so fond of (albeit spelled differently, which might merely demonstrate that in a region where every village has its own dialect and its own local identity, Morbach and Hermeskeil may well be on different planets): Gehaichnis. They can’t agree on its meaning. But Parvaneh’s young daughter Ava, who has listened in on the adults’ conversation, knows exactly what Gehaichnis means: lying in bed after her father has tucked her in with the door of her room left open.

Arguably, the fact that much of the dialogue in Die Lücken is in dialect adds to Bazyar’s credentials as a German (rather than hyphenated) author. But the most convincing act of appropriation is performed by Ava, who took the Hunsrück word Reitz and others had interpreted through the prism of the affectively loaded term Heimat, and found that it referred not to attachment to place but to attachment to family and to feeling safe at night.

But it’s Heimat, not Gehaichnis, that has interested reviewers. In a country where for the past ten years the centre of gravity of public discourse has moved a long way to the right, a book about village life by a German of Iranian extraction can be read as a much-needed riposte to conservative politicians waxing lyrically about traditional customs and costumes, not to mention far-right ideologues equating love for Heimat with love for an ethnically homogenous German fatherland.

Germans often do consider themselves Erinnerungsweltmeister, world champions of remembrance, and many have become convinced that Germany’s antisemitism was imported by migrants from Muslim countries who don’t appreciate the singularity of Auschwitz and need to be made to visit concentration camp memorials to teach them about “our” history. A book written by a migrant about the need to remember the Holocaust could therefore be seen as a timely intervention.

Yes, Bazyar’s novel is also about the Holocaust, but unlike many other fictional accounts of Germany’s Nazi past it lacks self-righteousness. That is not the least reason why Die Lücken is a great novel.

Anyway, it would be grossly unfair to welcome Shida Bazyar to the fold of German Erinnerungsweltmeister. Or to assume that Die Lücken could have a cathartic effect and make it possible to unproblematically reappropriate Heimat — in Hermeskeil and beyond. I can’t really think of a Heimat that has not been compromised, though maybe Bazyar is right: the term has become empty, and the need to come to grips with it overrated.

When I asked Heidenau residents a few years ago about the response to refugees in their town, they told me about the riots in 2015. Hardly anybody recalled that Heidenau had housed asylum seekers also in the 1990s and early 2000s. Their accommodation was often woefully inadequate. Some of them were people like Die Lücken’s Parvaneh — or like Shida Bazyar’s family, for that matter. Heidenau’s Iranians were comparatively well-educated and confident and particularly vocal in demanding decent living conditions. They and their activism have been forgotten; that’s an unfortunate Lücke in Heidenau’s collective memory.

There are also Lücken in Bazyar’s account of Heimesbach/Hermeskeil. Her readers encounter two refugee families, both of them from Iran. But Hermeskeil has been transformed by refugees other than the odd family from Iran. Since 2015, it has accommodated more asylum seekers than almost any other town of a comparable size. Most of them live in former army barracks that can house 1000 asylum seekers, but some were put up in tents. In October 2023, the Hermeskeil reception centre housed 1630 asylum seekers and refugees — one for every four regular Hermeskeil residents.

It’s not Bazyar’s responsibility to write about that, nor the job of any other author of migrant background to engage with Germany’s migration history. But they do anyway: Bazyar, for example, in her second book, or Selim Özdogan in his new novel, which is promoted as — you might have guessed — a Heimatroman.

More writers of fiction, particularly those who identify as ethnic Germans, may want to turn their attention to issues of postwar racism and postwar Germany’s response to migrants and refugees. They could explore the two types of Lücken Bazyar writes about: there are the stories untold and incidents unremembered that need to be made public. Why and how were Die Lücken’s narrator and her sister not made to feel welcome in Heimesbach? And didn’t their departure perhaps also leave a “gaping Lücke in the air” — “as if something had been snatched from it”?

Gunter Demnig was motivated to commemorate the Auschwitz Decree partly because of a controversy in the early 1990s over attempts to deport Romani migrants who had come to Germany during and in the aftermath of the Balkan wars, often because they were persecuted in Yugoslavia’s successor states. Many of them were living in Cologne, where a Romani community had emerged in the mid-1980s.

Much as Demnig’s initiative was informed by his response to racist policies and practices at the time, events in 2015 motivated Hildesheim resident Marco Boltz to initiate the laying of the first Stolperstein in his native Heidenau. Boltz, born in the late 1970s, was appalled by the racist riots in Heidenau that made Angela Merkel remind Germans at the time of the Constitution’s Article 1 (1): “Human dignity shall be inviolable.”

At last month’s award ceremony for the German Book Prize, Shida Bazyar drew attention to the rise of antisemitic and racist hate crimes. “At the moment, there is no minority [in Germany] that does not have reason for concern,” she said.

The failure — or refusal — to remember what had happened to the Ackermanns and the Samuels, and why, needs to be seen in the context of Germany’s endemic racism. Yet expectations that it, in turn, would fade away if only the Erinnerungsweltmeister put up enough memorials have proven unfounded. So have hopes for an unsullied German Heimat. •
